title: Reorder List
directAnswer: Reorder L0→L1→…→Ln into L0→Ln→L1→Ln-1→… in three in-place phases: (1) find the middle with slow/fast pointers, (2) reverse the second half, (3) merge the two halves by alternating nodes. Each phase is a linear pass, so the whole thing is O(n) time and O(1) space — no array, no node allocation.

remember.pattern: Find middle (slow/fast) → reverse second half → interleave merge
remember.formula:
# 1. middle
slow=fast=head
while fast.next and fast.next.next: slow=slow.next; fast=fast.next.next
# 2. reverse second half from slow.next
second=slow.next; slow.next=None; prev=None
while second: nxt=second.next; second.next=prev; prev=second; second=nxt
# 3. merge first half (head) with reversed second (prev)
first=head; second=prev
while second: t1=first.next; t2=second.next; first.next=second; second.next=t1; first=t1; second=t2
rules: Cut the list: after finding the middle, set `slow.next = None` so the first half terminates cleanly.
The first half is the **same length or one longer** than the second — that's why the merge loop ends when the reversed second half runs out.
Save **both** `next` pointers (`first.next` and `second.next`) before relinking in the merge, or you lose track of the rest.
Use the `fast.next && fast.next.next` middle so for even lengths `slow` lands on the **end of the first half** (the first half gets the extra node).
It's three textbook subroutines glued together — middle-finding, reversal, merge — don't try to do it in one clever pass.
whenToUse: Rearrange a singly linked list by interleaving its front and back
Any problem decomposable into find-middle + reverse + merge on a list
Palindrome checks and fold/zip operations on linked lists
When O(1) space is required and you can't dump nodes into an array
antiSignals: O(n) extra space is acceptable and clarity matters more → dump nodes into an array and two-pointer by index
It's a doubly linked list → you can walk backwards directly, no reversal needed
You only need to read, not rewrite, the order → just traverse with two indices
remember.takeaway: Reorder List is the canonical 'compose three linked-list primitives' problem. If you've drilled find-middle, reverse, and merge separately, this is just gluing them — which is exactly what the interviewer is checking.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you can decompose a compound list transformation into the three known subroutines and execute each in place without losing pointers — the integration test of linked-list fundamentals.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Forgetting to sever the first half (slow.next = null), creating a cycle; or mishandling the merge's saved-next pointers; or using the wrong middle so halves are mismatched.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Name the three phases up front, justify which half keeps the extra node for odd/even lengths, do it in O(1) space, and mention the O(n)-space array version as the simpler-but-heavier alternative.

problemStatement:
You are given the head of a singly linked list. The list can be represented as:

L0 → L1 → … → Ln-1 → Ln

Reorder the list to be in the following form:

L0 → Ln → L1 → Ln-1 → L2 → Ln-2 → …

You may not modify the values in the list's nodes. Only the nodes themselves may be changed.
constraints: The number of nodes is in the range [1, 5 × 10⁴]
You must reorder by relinking nodes, not by swapping values
understanding: We weave the list onto itself: first node, then last, then second, then second-to-last, and so on. The result is achieved purely by relinking nodes (values stay attached to their nodes). The ideal solution touches no extra memory beyond a few pointers.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can I modify the node links, or only the values?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: The prompt forbids changing values — I must relink the actual nodes. That rules out the lazy 'copy values into an array and overwrite' shortcut.

clarifyingQuestions.question: For an even-length list, which half gets the extra node?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: I'll let the first half hold the extra node (slow stops at the end of the first half), so the reversed second half is the shorter one driving the merge loop.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is O(1) space required or is O(n) acceptable?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: I'll target O(1) space with the three-phase in-place method, and mention the simpler O(n) array approach as a fallback if clarity is preferred.

clarifyingQuestions.question: What about a list with one or two nodes?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: One or two nodes are already in reordered form — the algorithm handles them as no-ops because the second half is empty or a single node.

examples.explanation: First half [1,2], reversed second half [4,3], interleaved: 1,4,2,3.
Odd length: first half [1,2,3], reversed tail [5,4]; interleave to 1,5,2,4,3 — the middle node 3 ends up last.
Two nodes are already in the target form; the reversed second half has one node and merging changes nothing.

diagrams.title: Picking the right approach
diagrams.caption: Three-phase in-place is the O(1)-space winner; the array method trades memory for less pointer juggling.

approaches.name: Array of Nodes — Two-Pointer by Index
approaches.whenToMention: Offer it first as the easy-to-reason-about baseline, then upgrade to the O(1)-space three-phase method.
hints: If you could randomly index the nodes like an array, reordering L0, Ln, L1, Ln-1 would just be reading from both ends inward. Linked lists lack random access — how do you fake it?
Walk the list once, pushing every node reference into an array. Now you have O(1) indexed access.
Use left=0 and right=n-1. Alternately attach nodes[left] then nodes[right], advancing inward, and remember to terminate the final node's next at null.
approaches.complexityReasoning: One pass to fill the array (O(n)) plus one pass with two indices to relink (O(n)). The array of n node references is O(n) extra space.
approaches.explanation:
We buy random access by copying node *references* into an array, then relink them in the reordered sequence using two indices converging from the ends.

**Why an array helps.** The target order L0, Ln, L1, Ln-1, … is trivially expressed as 'front, back, front+1, back-1, …' — but a singly linked list can't jump to the back. Dumping the n node references into an array gives O(1) access to any position, so the reorder becomes a simple two-pointer walk.

**The relink loop.** With `left` starting at 0 and `right` at n−1, we alternate: link `nodes[left]` to `nodes[right]`, then `nodes[right]` to `nodes[left+1]`, advancing `left++` and `right--`. We stop when the pointers meet, and finally set the last node's `next` to null so the list terminates instead of looping.

**Why we don't ship this as the headline.** It's correct and easy to explain, and the relinking is far less error-prone than in-place pointer surgery. But it spends O(n) memory storing references — which the cleaner three-phase method avoids entirely. State it as the baseline, then show you can do better.
approaches.insight: Storing node *references* (not values) is the key: we still relink the original nodes, satisfying the 'don't modify values' rule, while gaining array-style indexing. It's the honest, low-risk answer that sets up the O(1) optimization.

dryRun.intro: nodes = [n1, n2, n3, n4]; left=0, right=3 converge inward.

code.python:
def reorderList(self, head: ListNode) -> None:
    if not head or not head.next:
        return
    nodes = []
    cur = head
    while cur:
        nodes.append(cur)
        cur = cur.next
    left, right = 0, len(nodes) - 1
    while left < right:
        nodes[left].next = nodes[right]
        left += 1
        if left == right:
            break
        nodes[right].next = nodes[left]
        right -= 1
    nodes[left].next = None

java.explanation: Store node references (not values) so we can index them yet still relink originals.
Front node points to the current back node — the L0→Ln step.
Pointers met on an odd-length list; the middle node is the new tail.
Terminate the final node so the list doesn't loop back.

python.explanation: Collect references for O(1) indexed access.
Stop when the two indices collide (odd length).
Cut the tail to avoid a cycle.

pitfalls: Storing values instead of node references — then you'd be copying values, which the prompt forbids.
Forgetting to null-terminate the last node, leaving a cycle.
Off-by-one when left and right meet on odd-length lists.

approaches.name: In Place — Middle + Reverse + Merge (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The answer they want. Announce the three phases explicitly before coding so the interviewer can follow.
hints: The target weaves the back of the list into the front. What if you literally split the list in half and reversed the back half so its order matched the weave?
Phase 1: find the middle with slow/fast pointers. Phase 2: reverse the second half (the classic prev/curr/next flip). Phase 3: merge the two halves by alternating one node from each.
Cut the first half by setting slow.next = null before reversing. In the merge, save both lists' next pointers before relinking, and stop when the reversed second half is exhausted.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Three sequential linear passes — find middle, reverse, merge — sum to O(n). Each phase uses only a constant number of pointers, so O(1) extra space.
approaches.explanation:
We realise the interleaving by physically splitting, flipping, and zipping the list.

**Phase 1 — find the middle (slow/fast).** Advance `slow` by one and `fast` by two. Using the guard `fast.next && fast.next.next`, when `fast` stops, `slow` sits at the end of the first half. For even lengths this gives the first half the extra node, which is exactly what makes the later merge terminate cleanly.

**Phase 2 — reverse the second half.** Record `second = slow.next`, then **sever** the first half with `slow.next = null` so it terminates. Reverse the `second` chain with the standard three-pointer flip; `prev` ends as the head of the reversed back half. After this we have two independent lists: `head` (first half, in order) and `prev` (second half, reversed).

**Phase 3 — merge by alternating.** Walk both lists together. Each step, stash `t1 = first.next` and `t2 = second.next`, then weave: `first.next = second; second.next = t1`. Advance `first = t1` and `second = t2`. The reversed second half is the same length or one shorter than the first half, so the loop naturally ends when `second` becomes null, leaving the first half's final node correctly terminating the list.

**Why the lengths line up.** Because Phase 1 gives the first half the extra node on even lengths (and the exact middle on odd lengths), the second (reversed) half never overruns the first. That's the invariant that lets us drive the merge by 'while second != null' without a dangling pointer.
approaches.insight: The problem is not one clever algorithm — it's three boring ones composed correctly. The art is the bookkeeping: sever the halves so you don't build a cycle, and save both next-pointers in the merge so you don't strand a chain. Master each primitive alone and Reorder List is free.

dryRun.intro: Three phases: find middle, reverse tail, merge alternately.

code.python:
def reorderList(self, head: ListNode) -> None:
    if not head or not head.next:
        return

    # Phase 1: find the middle
    slow = fast = head
    while fast.next and fast.next.next:
        slow = slow.next
        fast = fast.next.next

    # Phase 2: reverse the second half
    second = slow.next
    slow.next = None
    prev = None
    while second:
        nxt = second.next
        second.next = prev
        prev = second
        second = nxt

    # Phase 3: merge the two halves
    first, second = head, prev
    while second:
        t1, t2 = first.next, second.next
        first.next = second
        second.next = t1
        first, second = t1, t2

java.explanation: This guard makes slow stop at the END of the first half, giving the first half the extra node on even lengths.
Head of the second half, before we sever it.
Cut the list into two independent halves; without this the merge builds a cycle.
Standard three-pointer reversal of the second half; prev becomes its new head.
Save both next-pointers BEFORE relinking, or we lose the rest of each chain.
Reversed second half is ≤ first half, so its exhaustion ends the merge with the list correctly terminated.

python.explanation: Stops slow at the end of the first half (first half keeps the extra node when even).
Grab the second half before cutting.
Sever the halves to avoid a cycle during the merge.
Reverse pointer flip; prev ends as the reversed second-half head.
Save both successors before weaving the nodes.
Advance both pointers; loop ends when second is None.

edgeCases.behavior: Guard returns immediately (head.next == null); a single node is already reordered.
slow stays at node 1, second half is [2] reversed to [2], merge links 1→2 → unchanged.
slow stops at node 2, second half [3,4]→[4,3], merge → 1→4→2→3.

pitfalls: Forgetting slow.next = null — the two halves stay connected and the merge creates a cycle.
Not saving both next-pointers in the merge — you strand one of the chains.
Using the wrong middle guard so the second half is longer than the first, overrunning the merge.

commonMistakes: Not severing the first half (slow.next = null) before reversing, which creates a cycle on merge.
Losing pointers during the merge by relinking before saving first.next and second.next.
Copying values instead of relinking nodes — the prompt explicitly forbids changing values.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Building a cycle by not cutting the list
commonMistakesDetailed.why: If slow.next still points into the second half when you merge, the reordered list loops back on itself forever.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
second = slow.next
# forgot: slow.next = None
prev = None
while second:
    nxt = second.next
    second.next = prev
    prev = second
    second = nxt
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
second = slow.next
slow.next = None   # sever the halves first
prev = None
while second:
    nxt = second.next
    second.next = prev
    prev = second
    second = nxt

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Stranding a chain in the merge
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Relinking first.next = second before saving the old first.next loses the rest of the first half.
